newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks hammered by inflation worries.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks hammered by inflation worries.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks nosedived Friday after economic data stirred fears of another Federal Reserve interest rate hike and as long-term interest rates hit their highest levels since July.

The dollar edged higher against the Japanese yen and German mark. In commodity markets, wheat prices soared to their highest closing price in more than six months against a background of unseasonably cold weather.
The Dow Jones industrial average plunged 148.36 points, or 2.27 percent, to 6,391.69. It was off 134.38 points for the week, its fifth straight down week.
The last time the index racked up such a string of declining weeks was in the last quarter of 1991.
In the broader market, declining issues swamped advances 2,322 to 379 on moderate volume of 440 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
A surprising jump in underlying wholesale prices in March forced investors to recast their outlook for inflation and interest rates.
The Labour Department said the Producer Price Index fell 0.1 percent in March, but the underlying rate, excluding often-volatile food and energy costs, rose an unexpected 0.4 precent.
Analysts said that rise, far higher than the 0.1 percent economists had forecast, meant the Federal Reserve was likely to become more aggressive in raising interest rates.

"This increases the odds of a Fed tightening very dramatically in May," said Pierre Ellis, senior international economist at Primark Decision Economics. "A 50-basis point (one-half percentage point) move is definitely on the table and the Fed almost looks behind the curve."

In the inflation-sensitive Treasury bond market, the benchmark 30-year bond fell 21/32, or $6.56 on a $1,000 bond. Its yield jumped to 7.17 percent -- the highest since July 8 during the stock market's last big slump -- from 7.11 percent Thursday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
As in July, analysts are again concerned about the implications of a surprisingly strong, persistent pace of economic growth.

"There's a cycle out there and it's accelerating," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "It's looking more and more like a boom to be followed at some time later by a bust."
Regardless of what comes next, the market's recent woes rank as some of the worst it has endured since embarking on its stunning ascent in early 1995.
Since its last record close of 7,085.16 on March 11, the Dow is off 693 points or nearly 9.8 percent, within a whisker of the 10 percent customarily considered to represent a significant correction.
The market's drop for the week was the first time since late 1991 that the average has fallen for five straight weeks.
Expectations of higher interest rates pushed the dollar higher against the yen and the mark, but that factor was offset by the stock market's drop.
The dollar closed at 1.7205 marks compared with 1.7190 marks Thursday and at 126.12 yen compared with 125.85 yen.
While higher interest rates generally support a stronger dollar, the sell-off in stocks led to concern that investors might unload dollar-denominated assets and sell dollars.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat for May delivery closed 10 cents a bushel higher at $4.03, its highest closing price since September 27, 1996.

Traders said this week's blast of freezing cold and snows from the Dakotas to Texas had grown into a threat to winter wheat planted last fall and now struggling to emerge. The crop is harvested in June and July.

In overseas markets, the FTSE 100 index closed 42.5 points lower at 4,270.7, wiping out the gains of the past two sessions and leaving the index up just 34.1 points on the week. The Nikkei 225 index closed up 361.23 points at 17,846.98 but down 13.61 on the week.
